title: Silk Route month by month: weather, views and crowds
meta_description: Old Silk Route month by month: snow, rhododendrons, monsoon fog, clear autumn views, temperatures at Zuluk and Nathang, crowds and prices for all 12 months.
summary: The best months for the Old Silk Route are mid-October to early December for clear views, January to March for snow, and April to May for rhododendrons. June to mid-September brings fog, rain and landslides. Puja, Diwali and New Year weeks are the most crowded and expensive. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The year at a glance
paras: The Silk Route runs from about 1,500 m at Lingtam to about 4,000 m at Nathang and Kupup, so one month can mean warm afternoons by the river and frozen pipes on the plateau. The table gives a quick sense of each month; the sections that follow explain the seasons in more detail. Temperatures are rough typical ranges for Zuluk at about 2,900 m and Nathang at about 4,000 m, not records, and every year is different.

Two things matter more than the temperature figures. The first is cloud: in most months the mornings are clearer than the afternoons, so the timing of your Thambi or Lungthung visit often decides what you see. The second is the road: snow in winter and slides in the monsoon can close the high road for a day or more, so the months with the most dramatic conditions also need the most flexible plans. Our ratings weigh views, road reliability and comfort together for a first-time visitor.

sections.heading: January and February: the snow months
paras: This is the season of the white zig-zag. Nathang and Kupup are usually under snow, Kupup's Elephant Lake freezes, and Zuluk and Thambi get their heaviest falls. On clear days the light is sharp and the views of Kangchenjunga from Thambi and Lungthung are excellent. The cost is cold and uncertainty: nights at Nathang fall to around −10 to −15 °C, water freezes, and the road above Zuluk can close for a day or more after a heavy fall until the Border Roads Organisation clears it.

Plan a spare day, choose a high-clearance car whose driver carries chains, and sleep at Zuluk rather than Nathang if anyone in the group is young, older or unsure about altitude. Crowds are thin except in the last week of December and the first days of January. Read our Silk Route in winter guide before booking.

sections.heading: March to May: thaw, flowers and haze
paras: March is a month of change. Late snowfalls are common up high, while the lower forest around Padamchen begins to show its first rhododendrons. By April the bloom has climbed towards Zuluk, and in May it reaches Thambi, Lungthung and the slopes near Nathang. Days are mild at Zuluk, around 15–17 °C, and even Nathang has comfortable afternoons, though nights stay cold.

The trade-off is visibility. Clear mornings are common, but haze and cloud build by late morning and often hide the snow peaks. Start early each day and enjoy the forests in the afternoon. This is a good season for families, since roads are usually open and the cold is manageable, and for anyone who wants flowers more than panoramas. School-holiday weeks in May get busy.

sections.heading: June to mid-September: the monsoon
paras: The south-west monsoon usually reaches Sikkim in early June and stays until mid-September. The Silk Route spends much of this time inside cloud. Rain is heavy on the forested lower road, landslides cut the Rongli–Zuluk road and NH10 between Siliguri and Rangpo, and leeches are active in the forest. Views of the loops and the snow peaks are rare, though the hills are a deep green and occasional clear mornings can be beautiful.

We do not recommend first visits in July and August. If your dates are fixed in these months, stay low, at Aritar, Rolep or Padamchen, and go up only on a promising morning. Prices are at their lowest, and homestays are quiet. Use the Kalimpong–Pedong–Rhenock road when NH10 is closed. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Late September to December: the clear season
paras: As the monsoon withdraws in late September, the air clears and the Silk Route enters its best season. October and November bring the most reliable views of the year: Kangchenjunga from Thambi on most mornings, the loops sharp against brown slopes, deep blue skies over Nathang. Days are crisp at Zuluk, nights cold, and the plateau has its first frosts and sometimes early snow by November.

This is also the busiest time. Durga Puja, Lakshmi Puja and Diwali bring large numbers of travellers from West Bengal and the rest of India, and homestays, cars and permits are in high demand. Book three to four weeks ahead for those weeks, or travel in the first half of November when the crowds thin. December stays clear and gets colder, with snow arriving at Nathang and Kupup, and the Christmas–New Year week is busy again.

sections.heading: Matching the month to your trip
paras: Different travellers want different things from the Silk Route. Here is how we match months to people when they ask us:
list: First visit, want the classic views: mid-October to early December, avoiding Puja week if you can.
Snow is the goal: mid-January to late February, with a spare day built in.
Flowers and mild days: April for the lower forests, May for the upper slopes.
Travelling with young children or older parents: March to May or October to November, sleeping at Padamchen or Zuluk.
Photographers: November for clarity, February for snow, May for rhododendrons; avoid July and August.
Lowest prices: late June to mid-September, if your dates are flexible and you accept fog and slides.
Quiet and clear together: the first half of November, or February outside long weekends.

sections.heading: Prices and booking through the year
paras: Silk Route prices move with demand rather than with the official season. Car rates and some homestay rates rise by roughly ₹500–1,000 a day in Durga Puja and Diwali weeks, over Christmas and New Year, and on spring long weekends. In these weeks book three to four weeks ahead, because the best homestays at Zuluk and the most experienced drivers fill first. Permit queues at Rongli are also longest then.

Outside those weeks you can usually book a week or two ahead. February, early March and the first half of November give good conditions at normal prices. The monsoon months are the cheapest of the year, and some homestays offer lower rates for longer stays, but you pay in uncertainty. Whatever the month, ask for a quote that names each night's stay, the vehicle and what happens if snow or a slide costs you a day.

sections.heading: Festivals, holidays and crowds
paras: Crowds on the Silk Route follow India's holiday calendar more than the weather. Durga Puja and the weeks around it, usually in October, are the busiest, followed by Diwali, the Christmas–New Year week and long weekends in spring. Losar, the Tibetan New Year in February or March, is celebrated in the region's Buddhist households and monasteries. Local festivals are small and family-centred rather than tourist events; if you are invited to join, accept with thanks and follow your host's lead.

Whatever the month, a few rules hold. Start early each day, because mornings are clearer than afternoons in every season. Keep one flexible day in winter and the monsoon. And check road and permit status with your driver or homestay before each high day, because conditions on the Silk Route change faster than any guide can.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Mid-October to early December for clear views of the zig-zag and Kangchenjunga; mid-January to late February for snow; April and May for rhododendrons. Avoid July and August, when fog, heavy rain and landslides are common. The first half of November is often the best balance of clear weather and smaller crowds.

faqs.q: Is October good for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Yes, October is one of the best months, with clear post-monsoon skies, crisp days at Zuluk and cold nights at Nathang. It is also the busiest month because of Durga Puja and Diwali holidays, so book homestays, cars and permits three to four weeks ahead. Late September can still have rain; from mid-October the weather is usually reliable.

faqs.q: Can I visit the Silk Route in June?
faqs.a: You can, but expect monsoon conditions: fog, rain, landslides on the Rongli–Zuluk road and NH10, and few clear views. Early June can still offer some good mornings. Keep flexible dates, stay low at Aritar or Padamchen if the weather is bad, and check road status each morning. Prices are at their lowest.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom on the Silk Route?
faqs.a: The bloom follows altitude. Lower forests around Padamchen flower from March into April, Zuluk in April, and Thambi, Lungthung and the slopes near Nathang in May, sometimes into early June. Late April to mid-May is usually the best overlap. A late snow or warm spring can shift the timing by a few weeks.

faqs.q: Is December a good time for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Yes. December usually brings clear, cold days with the first lasting snow at Nathang and Kupup, while Zuluk is cold but often snow-free. Nights at Nathang fall to around −10 °C. The Christmas–New Year week is busy and pricier. Carry proper winter clothing and keep a spare day in case of snow on the road.

faqs.q: How cold is Zuluk in November?
faqs.a: Days at Zuluk in November are usually around 10–12 °C and nights near freezing, while Nathang, about 1,100 m higher, falls to around −6 °C at night. Skies are mostly clear, so mornings are cold but bright. Pack thermals, a down or padded jacket, a cap and gloves, especially for sunrise at Thambi.

faqs.q: Which months should I avoid for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: July and August are the hardest months, with heavy rain, persistent fog and frequent landslides. June and early September are also risky. In winter, heavy snow can close the road for a day or more, so January and February need flexible plans rather than avoidance. Check current status before you travel in any month.

faqs.q: When is the Silk Route least crowded?
faqs.a: The quietest good-weather windows are the first half of November after Diwali, February outside long weekends, and early March. The monsoon months are quietest of all but come with fog and slides. The busiest periods are Durga Puja and Diwali weeks, Christmas to New Year and spring school holidays.

faqs.q: Does the Silk Route have snow in March?
faqs.a: Often at Nathang and Kupup, which usually stay white into March, and sometimes at Zuluk and Thambi after a late fall. March can bring some of the heaviest snow of the year in certain years, along with mild sunny days. Lower villages are snow-free, with early rhododendrons. Check recent conditions before you go.
